mainEntity.name: What is exception handling in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Exception handling in Java is a mechanism to deal with runtime errors gracefully — preventing abnormal program termination. When an exceptional condition occurs (file not found, null pointer dereference, division by zero), Java creates an exception object describing the error and 'throws' it. The program can 'catch' this exception and take corrective action. Java provides five keywords: try (wraps risky code), catch (handles specific exceptions), finally (always executes for cleanup), throw (manually throws an exception), and throws (declares checked exceptions a method may throw).

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between checked and unchecked exceptions?

acceptedAnswer.text: Checked exceptions extend Exception (but not RuntimeException) and MUST be either caught or declared with 'throws' at compile time. The compiler enforces handling. Examples: IOException, SQLException, ParseException. They represent recoverable conditions the caller should anticipate. Unchecked exceptions extend RuntimeException and do NOT need explicit handling — they represent programming errors. Examples: NullPointerException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, IllegalArgumentException, ClassCastException. Errors (OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError) are a third category — represent JVM-level failures, generally not recoverable.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between throw and throws in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: 'throw' is a statement used to explicitly create and throw an exception object from within a method: 'throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid input")'. 'throws' is a keyword in the method signature that DECLARES which checked exceptions the method might propagate to the caller: 'public void readFile(String path) throws IOException'. 'throw' is the action; 'throws' is the declaration. A method can throw an exception without using 'throws' if the exception is unchecked (RuntimeException subclass).

mainEntity.name: Does finally block always execute in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: The finally block executes in almost all cases — whether an exception occurs or not, whether it is caught or not, even when a return statement is encountered in the try or catch block. Three rare exceptions where finally does NOT execute: (1) System.exit() is called — JVM shuts down immediately. (2) JVM crashes (e.g., kill -9 on Unix). (3) The thread executing the try-catch is killed forcibly. Finally is used for resource cleanup (closing connections, streams) to guarantee cleanup happens regardless of what the try block does.

try-with-resources (Java 7+) automatically closes resources that implement AutoCloseable (or Closeable) when the try block exits — whether normally or via exception. Syntax: 'try (ResourceType res = new ResourceType()) { ... }'. Multiple resources can be declared, separated by semicolons, and are closed in REVERSE order of declaration. This eliminates the need for explicit finally blocks for resource cleanup and handles the tricky case where both the try block body and the close() method throw exceptions (the close() exception becomes suppressed).

sections.title: What is an Exception in Java?

blocks.text: An exception in Java is an unexpected event that disrupts the normal flow of a program during execution. When a problematic situation arises — a file that does not exist, a null reference being dereferenced, an invalid array index, a network connection timeout — the Java runtime creates an exception object that encapsulates information about the error: its type, a descriptive message, and the stack trace showing exactly where in the code it occurred.

Without exception handling, any runtime error immediately terminates the entire program — a poor user experience and a reliability disaster for production systems. Java's exception handling mechanism allows programs to detect these conditions, respond intelligently, log the problem, and continue operating — or shut down gracefully with a meaningful error message — rather than crashing without explanation.

Java uses five keywords for exception handling: try — wraps the risky code that might throw an exception; catch — handles a specific exception type; finally — always executes, regardless of outcome, used for cleanup; throw — manually creates and throws an exception; throws — declares in the method signature that a method may propagate a checked exception to its caller.

blocks.title: 🔑 Exception vs Error — Critical Distinction
blocks.text: Java distinguishes two categories of serious runtime problems: EXCEPTIONS are conditions that a well-written program can and should anticipate and recover from — file not found, invalid input, network timeout. ERRORS represent catastrophic JVM-level failures that programs generally cannot recover from — OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError, VirtualMachineError. The rule of thumb: catch Exceptions (and handle them meaningfully), never catch Errors (they signal the JVM itself is in trouble). Both Exception and Error extend the common superclass Throwable.

sections.title: Exception Hierarchy — The Complete Throwable Tree

blocks.text: Java's exception mechanism is built on a class hierarchy rooted at java.lang.Throwable. Every exception and error in Java is an instance of Throwable or one of its subclasses. Understanding this hierarchy is fundamental to writing correct exception handling code — because catch blocks use IS-A matching, catching a parent type also catches all its subclasses.

items.title: Throwable (Root)
items.text: java.lang.Throwable is the root of all exception and error types. It provides: getMessage() — descriptive error message, getCause() — the original exception that caused this one, getStackTrace() — array of stack frames, printStackTrace() — prints the full call stack to stderr. Only Throwable instances (and subclasses) can be thrown with 'throw' and caught with 'catch'.

items.title: Exception Branch
items.text:
java.lang.Exception represents conditions a program should anticipate and recover from. Two major subtrees:
• Checked Exceptions: extend Exception directly (not via RuntimeException). Compiler enforces handling. Examples: IOException, SQLException, ClassNotFoundException, ParseException.
• Unchecked Exceptions: extend RuntimeException. No compiler enforcement. Examples: NullPointerException, IllegalArgumentException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

items.title: Error Branch
items.text:
java.lang.Error represents severe, typically unrecoverable JVM-level failures. Should NEVER be caught in normal application code. Examples:
• OutOfMemoryError — heap exhausted
• StackOverflowError — infinite recursion
• NoClassDefFoundError — class missing at runtime
• AssertionError — assertion failed
• VirtualMachineError — JVM internal error
If you see these in production, they indicate infrastructure or code architecture problems — not logic bugs to catch.

sections.title: try-catch-finally — The Foundation of Exception Handling

blocks.text: The try-catch-finally construct is the core mechanism for handling exceptions in Java. The try block wraps code that might throw an exception. One or more catch blocks each handle a specific exception type. The optional finally block runs always — after normal completion or exception handling — making it the perfect place for cleanup code like closing resources.

items.title: try Block
items.text: Wraps the risky code — statements that might throw exceptions. The moment an exception is thrown inside try, execution jumps immediately to the matching catch block — remaining statements in the try block are skipped. If no exception occurs, all catch blocks are skipped and finally (if present) executes.

items.title: catch Block
items.text: Handles a specific exception type. Catches the exception and its subclasses (IS-A). Multiple catch blocks can follow one try — each handles a different exception type. Evaluated top-to-bottom — the FIRST matching catch block runs; all others are skipped. NEVER catch a more general type before a more specific one in the same try-catch — compile error (unreachable catch block).

items.title: finally Block
items.text: Executes ALWAYS — whether the try block completes normally, throws an exception that is caught, or throws an exception that is NOT caught. Even a return statement in try or catch does NOT prevent finally from running. Three exceptional cases: System.exit(), JVM crash, or thread death. Use finally for: closing file handles, releasing DB connections, unlocking resources.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Never Return from finally — It Swallows Exceptions
blocks.text: Placing a 'return' statement inside a finally block is a dangerous anti-pattern. If the try block throws an exception and the finally block contains a return, the exception is SILENTLY SWALLOWED — it disappears without any trace. The method returns normally as if nothing went wrong. This makes debugging extremely difficult. Rule: never use return, break, or continue in a finally block — only use finally for cleanup (close, unlock, release). The IDE IntelliJ IDEA warns: 'return inside finally block'.

blocks.text: Java uses two similar-looking keywords — throw and throws — that serve completely different purposes. Confusing them is one of the most common interview mistakes. Mastering both is essential for writing correct, self-documenting exception handling code.

sections.title: Checked vs Unchecked Exceptions — Know the Difference

blocks.text: Java's exception system is divided into checked and unchecked exceptions. This distinction profoundly affects how you write and call methods. The Java compiler actively participates in checked exception handling — it verifies at compile time that every checked exception is either handled or declared. Unchecked exceptions bypass this compiler check entirely.

Caller CAN and SHOULD handle it
Forces callers to think about failure paths

blocks.title: 💡 Modern Java Preference — Unchecked Exceptions
blocks.text: Major frameworks like Spring, Hibernate, and JUnit intentionally wrap checked exceptions in unchecked ones (Spring's DataAccessException wraps SQLException; JUnit's AssertionError is unchecked). The rationale: checked exceptions often pollute method signatures throughout a call stack, forcing every layer to either handle or re-declare exceptions it cannot meaningfully address. The modern Java consensus: use checked exceptions only for conditions where the caller has a realistic recovery strategy. For programming errors and conditions callers cannot recover from, use unchecked exceptions.

sections.title: Multi-catch & Exception Order — Catching Multiple Types

blocks.text: Java provides two patterns for catching multiple exception types: separate catch blocks (one per exception type) and multi-catch (Java 7+, multiple types in one block separated by |). Understanding the ordering rules prevents the most common multi-catch compile errors.

items.title: Catch Block Order Rules
items.text:
Catch blocks are evaluated TOP-TO-BOTTOM. The FIRST matching catch block runs — all remaining are skipped.
Rule: always place MORE SPECIFIC exceptions BEFORE LESS SPECIFIC ones.
Wrong order: catch(Exception e) before catch(IOException e) → compile error: 'exception IOException has already been caught'.
Correct order: specific first, general last. A 'catch (Exception e)' as the last catch is a common pattern to handle any unexpected exception.

items.title: Multi-catch (Java 7+) — The | Operator
items.text:
Syntax: catch (ExceptionA | ExceptionB | ExceptionC e)
When multiple exceptions need the SAME handling logic, multi-catch eliminates code duplication.
Constraint: the caught variable 'e' is implicitly final — cannot be reassigned inside the block.
Constraint: cannot use related types (parent and child) in the same multi-catch — compile error: 'type is already caught by the alternative'.
Benefit: cleaner code without repeating the same handler body.

items.title: Catching Throwable vs Exception
items.text:
catch(Exception e): catches all checked and unchecked exceptions — appropriate as a last resort fallback.
catch(Throwable t): catches Errors too — almost never appropriate. Errors (OutOfMemoryError etc.) signal JVM failure — catching them can hide serious problems or prevent proper JVM shutdown.
Rule: catch the most specific type you can meaningfully handle. Use catch(Exception e) sparingly as a global fallback. Never catch Throwable in normal application code.

blocks.text: try-with-resources (Java 7+, JEP 334 improved in Java 9) automatically closes resources that implement AutoCloseable (or its subinterface Closeable) when the try block exits — regardless of whether it exits normally or via exception. It is the recommended pattern for all resource management in modern Java, replacing the verbose and error-prone try-finally pattern.

items.title: How try-with-resources Works
items.text: Resources declared in the parentheses after 'try' are automatically closed when the try block exits. Close() is called in REVERSE order of declaration (last opened, first closed). If both the try body and close() throw exceptions, the body's exception propagates and the close() exception becomes a SUPPRESSED exception — accessible via getSuppressed(). This is the key advantage over try-finally.

items.title: Multiple Resources
Implementing AutoCloseable
items.text: Any class implementing AutoCloseable (one method: void close() throws Exception) works with try-with-resources. Implementing Closeable (throws IOException only) is more specific. Custom resources like DB connections, HTTP clients, thread pools should implement AutoCloseable to participate in try-with-resources. This is how modern Java resource management is designed.

blocks.text: Java's built-in exceptions cover general programming errors, but real applications need domain-specific exceptions that carry meaningful business context. A PaymentDeclinedException is far more informative than a generic RuntimeException. Custom exceptions make error handling code self-documenting, enable callers to react differently to different failure modes, and carry structured data about what went wrong.

items.title: Custom Exception Design Rules
items.text:
1. Choose the right superclass: extend RuntimeException for unchecked (most domain exceptions), extend Exception for checked (when callers should be forced to handle).
2. Always provide BOTH constructors: (String message) and (String message, Throwable cause) — cause enables exception chaining.
3. Add domain-specific fields for structured context: errorCode, orderId, userId, retryAfterSeconds.
4. Make fields final — exceptions should be immutable.
5. Follow the naming convention: end with 'Exception'.

items.title: Exception Hierarchy for Your Domain
items.text:
Group related exceptions under a base domain exception. This lets callers catch the entire category if they choose:
ApplicationException (base)
├── ValidationException
│   ├── InvalidEmailException
│   └── InvalidPhoneException
└── BusinessException
    ├── InsufficientFundsException
    └── AccountFrozenException
Callers can catch ValidationException to handle all validation failures, or InsufficientFundsException to handle just that specific case.

items.title: When to Create Custom Exceptions
items.text: Create custom exceptions when: (1) The exception needs domain-specific context (orderId, errorCode, retryAfterMs). (2) Callers need to distinguish this failure from others — different recovery strategies. (3) The built-in exception names don't clearly communicate the business situation. (4) You're building a library or SDK — custom exceptions create a stable API contract. Don't create custom exceptions for every method — use IllegalArgumentException, IllegalStateException for basic validation.

sections.title: Exception Chaining & Cause — Preserving Error Context

blocks.text: Exception chaining (also called exception wrapping) is the practice of catching a low-level exception and re-throwing it as a higher-level, more meaningful exception — while preserving the original exception as the cause. This is critical for debuggability: without the cause, the root problem is hidden; with it, the full chain of errors is visible in the stack trace.

items.title: Why Chain Exceptions
items.text: A service layer should not expose JDBC's SQLException to a UI layer. Instead, it catches SQLException and throws a domain-meaningful DatabaseException — but includes the original SQLException as the cause. The caller sees a BusinessException. But when debugging, getCause() retrieves the original SQLException with its full stack trace. This is the principle of 'translate, not suppress' — convert the exception type but never lose the original context.

items.title: Cause Constructor Pattern
Suppressed Exceptions
items.text: Java 7+ introduced addSuppressed(Throwable) for cases where multiple exceptions occur simultaneously — most commonly in try-with-resources where both the try body and close() throw. The primary exception propagates; the close() exception is suppressed but attached. getSuppressed() retrieves them. They appear in the stack trace as 'Suppressed:' entries, not as 'Caused by:'.

// Logs it here AND caller might log again — duplicate logs

sections.title: Exception Propagation — The Call Stack Journey

blocks.text: When an exception is thrown and not caught in the current method, it propagates up the call stack — the current method is exited immediately, its local variables are discarded, and the exception is passed to the calling method. This continues frame by frame until either a matching catch block is found or the exception reaches the JVM's main thread handler and the thread terminates.

items.title: Propagation Rules
items.text:
Unchecked exceptions propagate automatically — no declaration needed at each level.
Checked exceptions require either catch or throws declaration at each stack frame.
When a method declares 'throws CheckedException', it is telling the compiler: 'I'm not handling this, my caller must.'
The exception propagates until: (1) a catch block matches it, (2) it reaches main() and is uncaught, or (3) it reaches a thread's uncaught exception handler.

items.title: Reading a Stack Trace
items.text: A stack trace reads BOTTOM-UP for origin — the bottom line is where the exception originated; each line above it is a calling method. The top line is where the exception was caught (or the thread that died). Each line shows: ClassName.methodName(FileName.java:lineNumber). 'Caused by:' sections show the exception chain. 'Suppressed:' shows close() exceptions from try-with-resources.

items.title: Catch at the Right Level
items.text: The correct level to catch an exception is the level that has enough CONTEXT to handle it meaningfully. A data access method shouldn't catch its own SQLException and show a UI dialog — it has no UI context. The UI layer should catch and display appropriately. Repository layer: translate technical exceptions to domain exceptions. Service layer: handle business rule violations. Presentation layer: translate to user-friendly messages.

throw new java.io.IOException("Disk read failed at sector 47");
// Level 2 — middle — declares throws, does not catch

System.out.println("← Leaving level2 (no exception)"); // Never reached
// ★ Caught in level1: Disk read failed at sector 47
// This is how enterprise apps are SUPPOSED to handle exceptions
// Data Access Layer — translates SQL to domain exception
if (id == null) throw new java.sql.SQLException("Null parameter");
// Translate — don't expose JDBC to service layer
throw new DatabaseException("DB lookup failed for user: " + id, e);
// Service Layer — translates domain exception to business exception
throw new ServiceException("Cannot retrieve user profile", e);
// Controller Layer — translates to HTTP response or UI message
// Log with full cause chain, return user-friendly message
return "500 Internal Error: Unable to load profile";

sections.title: Common Java Exceptions Explained — What Causes Them & How to Fix

blocks.text: These are the exceptions you will encounter most frequently in Java development. Understanding exactly what triggers each one — and how to prevent or handle it — saves hours of debugging time.

rows: Calling a method or accessing a field on a null reference
Accessing arr[i] where i < 0 or i >= arr.length
Check arr.length before indexing; use enhanced for loops
Casting an object to a type it is not (fails instanceof check)
Check instanceof before casting; use generics to avoid casts
Integer.parseInt("abc") — string is not a valid number
Validate format before parsing; use try-catch for user input
Infinite recursion — no base case or base case never reached
Verify base case exists and is reachable; use iteration for deep recursion
JVM heap exhausted — too many objects or memory leak
Profile with VisualVM; fix leaks; increase heap with -Xmx if justified
Modifying a collection while iterating it with Iterator
Use Iterator.remove(); copy before modifying; use CopyOnWriteArrayList
Method received an argument that violates its contract
Validate inputs at method start; document preconditions clearly
Method called at a wrong time or in wrong object state
Check object state before calling; use state machine patterns
Operation not supported by this implementation
Check if collection is modifiable; use mutable collection types

sections.title: Common Mistakes & Pitfalls — Errors That Trip Everyone Up

blocks.text: These exception handling mistakes appear consistently in Java beginner and intermediate code. Each one either hides real problems, corrupts error context, or leads to resource leaks that only surface in production.

throw e; // Re-throw or throw a domain exception

System.out.println("Something went wrong"); // Which thing? Can't tell
// ❌ MISTAKE 3: Catching exception without the cause — losing root cause
throw new RuntimeException("Database error"); // ❌ Cause lost!
// ✅ Fix: always pass cause to new exception
throw new DatabaseException("Query failed: " + e.getMessage(), e); // ✅
// ❌ MISTAKE 4: Using exceptions for normal control flow
getUser(id); // throws UserNotFoundException if not found
return false; // ❌ Exception as conditional — expensive, poor design
// ✅ Fix: return Optional or design API to check first
public Optional<User> findUser(String id) { /* ... */ return Optional.empty(); }
// ❌ MISTAKE 5: re-declaring unchecked exceptions in throws
// Not an error, but misleading and unnecessary
public void setAge(int age) throws NullPointerException { // ❌ Unnecessary
// ✅ Fix: don't declare unchecked exceptions in throws (unless documenting)
// ❌ MISTAKE 6: Finally block with return statement
return 2; // ❌ Overrides try's return AND swallows any exception!
// Always returns 2, any exception in try is silently swallowed
// ❌ MISTAKE 7: Not closing resources in finally (before Java 7)

sections.title: Bad Practices & Anti-Patterns — What Senior Developers Reject

blocks.text: These exception handling anti-patterns are among the top reasons for failed code reviews in professional Java teams. Each one either hides bugs, corrupts logs, leaks resources, or makes systems impossible to diagnose in production.

items.title: Pokemon Exception Handling — Gotta Catch 'Em All
items.text: 'catch (Exception e) {}' — catching everything and doing nothing. Named after the game's 'catch all Pokémon' theme. This is the single most destructive exception handling pattern: bugs disappear without a trace, systems fail silently, and production issues become nearly impossible to diagnose. Rule: if you catch an exception, you must either handle it meaningfully or re-throw (with cause). An empty catch block should be a code review blocker.

items.title: Log-and-Throw (Duplicate Logging)
items.text: Logging the exception AND throwing it, causing the same error to appear multiple times in the logs — at every layer of the stack. Production log files become noisy, making real issues hard to spot. Fix: log at the TOP-MOST handler level only (where you can fully handle it). Let exceptions propagate silently through intermediate layers (just re-throw or chain). The boundary between application code and framework (Spring MVC, JAX-RS) is where logging belongs.

items.title: Using Exceptions for Control Flow
items.text: Throwing exceptions for expected, normal conditions — 'throw UserNotFoundException' to signal 'user not found' in a lookup. Exceptions have a significant performance cost (capturing the stack trace). They make code harder to read. They are meant for EXCEPTIONAL conditions — errors outside normal program flow. Use Optional<T>, null (carefully), or boolean flags for normal conditions. Reserve exceptions for genuinely exceptional situations.

items.title: Catching Throwable or Error
items.text: Catching Throwable or Error (OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError) in application code is almost always wrong. These errors signal JVM-level failures. Catching them can prevent proper JVM cleanup, hide catastrophic failures, make the system appear healthy when it's in an unrecoverable state. Spring's @ExceptionHandler and Tomcat's error pages handle unrecoverable errors at the framework level. Application code should only catch Exception at most.

items.title: Overusing Checked Exceptions
items.text: Declaring every possible checked exception in every method signature creates 'exception pollution' — methods that do nothing but pass checked exceptions up the call stack. This forces callers to handle exceptions they cannot meaningfully address. The Spring framework famously wraps all SQL exceptions in unchecked DataAccessException precisely because most callers cannot recover from a database failure. Design principle: checked exceptions for conditions callers CAN recover from; unchecked for everything else.

items.title: Missing Exception Context
items.text: throw new RuntimeException("error") — no context, no cause, no identifying information. When this appears in production logs, it is nearly impossible to diagnose. Always include: what failed, what the input/state was, and the cause exception. Good: 'throw new OrderProcessingException("Failed to save order #" + orderId + " for customer " + customerId, sqlException)'. Bad: 'throw new RuntimeException("Database error")'. Context is everything in production debugging.

sections.title: Java Exception Handling Interview Questions — Beginner to Advanced

blocks.text: These questions are consistently asked in Java fresher and experienced developer interviews, campus placements, and OCPJP certification exams.

items.q: Q1. What is the difference between checked and unchecked exceptions in Java?
items.a: Checked exceptions extend Exception (not RuntimeException) and MUST be either caught or declared with 'throws' in the method signature — the compiler enforces this. They represent recoverable external conditions: IOException, SQLException, ParseException. Unchecked exceptions extend RuntimeException — no compiler enforcement, optional to catch. They represent programming errors: NullPointerException, IllegalArgumentException, ClassCastException. Errors (OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError) are a third category extending Error — represent JVM failures, should never be caught. Rule: checked = 'caller can and should recover'. Unchecked = 'programming mistake or unrecoverable'.

items.q: Q2. What is the difference between throw and throws in Java?
items.a: 'throw' is a STATEMENT inside a method body that actually creates and throws an exception object: 'throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid age")'. It transfers control immediately to the nearest matching catch block. 'throws' is a KEYWORD in the METHOD SIGNATURE that DECLARES checked exceptions the method might propagate: 'void readFile(String path) throws IOException'. At runtime, throws does nothing — it is purely a compile-time declaration that tells callers what to handle. throw = action. throws = declaration. A method can throw unchecked exceptions without declaring them with throws.

items.q: Q3. Does the finally block always execute in Java? When does it NOT execute?
items.a: The finally block executes in virtually all circumstances: when the try block completes normally, when it throws a caught exception, when it throws an uncaught exception, and even when a return statement is encountered in try or catch (finally runs BEFORE the method actually returns). Three cases where finally does NOT execute: (1) System.exit() is called — JVM shuts down immediately without running any finally blocks. (2) The JVM process itself is killed forcibly (kill -9 on Linux). (3) The executing thread is stopped via deprecated Thread.stop() or the JVM crashes. For all practical purposes in normal application code — finally always runs.

items.q: Q4. What is exception chaining? Why is it important?
items.a: Exception chaining (introduced in Java 1.4) is wrapping a low-level exception inside a higher-level, more meaningful exception while preserving the original as the CAUSE. Example: catching a SQLException and throwing a DatabaseException(message, sqlException). The cause is stored via super(message, cause) and retrieved with getCause(). Importance: (1) Each layer translates to its own abstraction (JDBC → domain → service). (2) The root cause is never lost — the full chain appears in the stack trace as 'Caused by:'. (3) Callers interact with domain exceptions, not infrastructure details. Without chaining, exception wrapping swallows the original root cause — making production debugging nearly impossible.

items.q: Q5. What is try-with-resources? How is it better than try-finally?
items.a: try-with-resources (Java 7+) automatically closes resources implementing AutoCloseable when the try block exits. Syntax: 'try (Resource r = new Resource()) { }'. Advantages over try-finally: (1) SIMPLER CODE — no need for null checks in finally and nested try-catch to close the resource. (2) REVERSE CLOSE ORDER — multiple resources closed in reverse declaration order automatically. (3) SUPPRESSED EXCEPTIONS — if both try body and close() throw, the body exception propagates and close() exception is suppressed but accessible via getSuppressed() — no exception silently lost. With try-finally, if both throw, the finally's exception overwrites and loses the original. It is the recommended pattern for all resource management in modern Java.

items.q: Q6. Can we have a try block without catch or finally?
items.a: A try block CANNOT exist alone — it must be followed by either catch, finally, or both. Valid combinations: (1) try + catch (most common). (2) try + finally (no catch — exception still propagates, but finally cleans up). (3) try + catch + finally (complete form). (4) try-with-resources — can have no catch and no finally if the resource itself handles cleanup. INVALID: 'try { }' alone — compile error. Note: a try-with-resources can technically stand alone: 'try (res) { }' — the resource is closed but any exception propagates to the caller.

items.q:
Q7. What is the output?
try { return 1; } finally { return 2; }
items.a: Output: returns 2. The finally block ALWAYS executes before the method actually returns, even when a return statement is encountered in try. In this case, finally's 'return 2' OVERRIDES the try's 'return 1'. The method returns 2. If an exception were thrown in try and finally had 'return 2', the exception would be SILENTLY SWALLOWED — the method returns 2 as if nothing happened. This is a severe anti-pattern: returning from finally can hide exceptions and override earlier return values unexpectedly. IntelliJ IDEA warns: 'return inside finally block'. Never return (or throw) from a finally block.

items.q: Q8. What is the difference between Error and Exception in Java?
items.a: Both Error and Exception extend Throwable. Exception: represents conditions a program can anticipate and recover from — IOException, SQLException, NullPointerException. Catching and handling exceptions is normal, expected programming. Error: represents serious, typically unrecoverable JVM or system-level failures — OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError, NoClassDefFoundError, AssertionError. These signal infrastructure problems, JVM crashes, or catastrophic situations. Application code should NEVER catch Error. If you encounter Errors in production, they indicate architecture problems (memory leaks, infinite recursion), insufficient resources (heap too small), or environment issues — not application logic bugs to handle with try-catch.

items.q: Q9. Can we write a custom exception in Java? What are the best practices?
items.a: Yes. Custom exceptions are created by extending Exception (checked) or RuntimeException (unchecked). Best practices: (1) Extend RuntimeException for most domain exceptions (modern Java favours unchecked). (2) Always provide at least two constructors: (String message) and (String message, Throwable cause) — the cause constructor is essential for exception chaining. (3) Add domain-specific fields for structured context: errorCode, entityId, retryAfterSeconds. Make them final — exceptions should be immutable. (4) Create a hierarchy for your domain: base AppException → ValidationException, BusinessException → InsufficientFundsException. (5) Name ending with 'Exception'. (6) Use custom exceptions when the built-in types don't convey sufficient domain meaning or when callers need different recovery logic per exception type.

items.q: Q10. What happens when an exception is thrown in a catch block?
items.a: If an exception is thrown INSIDE a catch block (not re-throwing the original), the original exception is effectively replaced. The new exception propagates up the call stack looking for a matching handler. If a finally block is present, it executes before the new exception propagates — just as it would for any exception in the try block. If the catch block CATCHES the original and then throws a new exception WITHOUT chaining (without passing original as cause), the original exception is lost forever — this is the 'swallowing with replacement' anti-pattern. Always chain: 'throw new ServiceException("message", originalException)' to preserve the root cause.

Output: 2. The finally block's 'return 2' OVERRIDES the try block's 'return 1'. Even though try executes 'return 1' first, the JVM notes the pending return but runs finally before actually returning. The finally's 'return 2' becomes the effective return value. This demonstrates why returning from finally is an anti-pattern — it silently discards the try's return value. If an exception had been thrown in try, 'return 2' in finally would have silently swallowed that exception too.

COMPILE ERROR: 'exception IOException has already been caught'. IOException is a subclass of Exception. The catch(Exception e) block already catches IOException (and all Exception subclasses). The subsequent catch(IOException e) is unreachable — a more specific exception cannot follow a more general one that already catches it. Fix: reverse the order — put catch(IOException e) BEFORE catch(Exception e). Rule: always order catch blocks from MOST SPECIFIC to LEAST SPECIFIC. The compiler enforces this to prevent dead catch blocks.

items.q: 7. What is the difference between suppressed exceptions and cause exceptions? Give an example showing both.
items.a: CAUSE exception: the original exception that caused the current one. Set via constructor 'new Exception(msg, cause)'. Retrieved with getCause(). Appears as 'Caused by:' in stack traces. Represents a translation chain from low-level to high-level. SUPPRESSED exception: an additional exception that occurred while another was already propagating — most common from close() in try-with-resources. Added via addSuppressed(). Retrieved with getSuppressed(). Appears as 'Suppressed:' in stack traces. Example: // Suppressed: try (AutoCloseable r = () -> { throw new Exception("close failed"); }) { throw new RuntimeException("try failed"); } catch (Exception e) { System.out.println("Primary: " + e.getMessage()); // try failed System.out.println("Suppressed: " + e.getSuppressed()[0].getMessage()); // close failed } // Cause: catch (SQLException e) { throw new DatabaseException("DB error", e); // e becomes the cause } catch (DatabaseException e) { System.out.println(e.getCause().getMessage()); // the original SQLException }

items.q: 8. Write a generic retry utility method that retries a Supplier<T> up to maxRetries times, with exponential backoff, and throws a custom RetryExhaustedException if all retries fail.
items.a: public class RetryUtils { @FunctionalInterface public interface ThrowingSupplier<T> { T get() throws Exception; } public static <T> T withRetry(ThrowingSupplier<T> supplier, int maxRetries, long initialDelayMs) { Exception lastException = null; for (int attempt = 1; attempt <= maxRetries; attempt++) { try { return supplier.get(); } catch (Exception e) { lastException = e; if (attempt < maxRetries) { long delay = initialDelayMs * (1L << (attempt - 1)); // Exponential: 1x, 2x, 4x... System.out.printf("Attempt %d/%d failed: %s. Retrying in %dms%n", attempt, maxRetries, e.getMessage(), delay); try { Thread.sleep(delay); } catch (InterruptedException ie) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); throw new RetryExhaustedException("Retry interrupted after " + attempt + " attempts", ie); } } } } throw new RetryExhaustedException( "All " + maxRetries + " attempts failed", lastException); } } class RetryExhaustedException extends RuntimeException { RetryExhaustedException(String msg, Throwable cause) { super(msg, cause); } } // Usage: String result = RetryUtils.withRetry(() -> httpClient.get(url), 3, 500);

sections.title: Conclusion — Exception Handling: The Mark of Production-Ready Code

blocks.text: Exception handling is not an afterthought — it is a first-class design concern. The difference between code that works in a demo and code that works reliably in production is often entirely in how exceptions are handled. Programs that crash on the first bad input, silently swallow errors, or produce unhelpful 'Something went wrong' messages are not production-ready, regardless of how correct the happy path is.

Professional Java developers think about exceptions at the design level: What can go wrong here? Can the caller recover? Should this be checked or unchecked? What context does the exception need to carry for diagnosis? They use try-with-resources universally for resources, chain exceptions to preserve root causes, create meaningful custom exception hierarchies, and catch at the layer that has sufficient context to handle meaningfully.

faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions — Java Exception Handling

items.q: What is exception handling in Java?
items.a: Exception handling in Java is a mechanism to deal with runtime errors gracefully — preventing abnormal program termination. Five keywords: try (wraps risky code), catch (handles specific exceptions), finally (always executes for cleanup), throw (manually throws an exception), and throws (declares checked exceptions in method signature). When an exception is thrown, Java creates an exception object and searches up the call stack for a matching catch block.

items.q: What is the difference between checked and unchecked exceptions?
items.a: Checked exceptions extend Exception (not RuntimeException) and must be caught or declared with 'throws' — compiler enforces handling. They represent recoverable external conditions: IOException, SQLException. Unchecked exceptions extend RuntimeException — no compiler enforcement — represent programming errors: NullPointerException, IllegalArgumentException. Errors (OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError) are a third category for JVM-level failures — should never be caught.

items.q: What is the difference between throw and throws in Java?
items.a: 'throw' is a statement that actually creates and throws an exception object from inside a method body. 'throws' is a keyword in the method signature that declares which checked exceptions the method may propagate to callers. throw = action (happens at runtime). throws = declaration (compile-time contract). A method can throw unchecked exceptions without declaring them in throws.

items.q: Does finally block always execute in Java?
items.a: The finally block executes in virtually all circumstances — whether try completes normally, throws a caught exception, or throws an uncaught exception. Even return statements in try or catch don't prevent finally from running. Three exceptions: System.exit() is called, JVM crashes, or thread is forcibly killed. For normal application code — finally always runs. Never use return or throw in finally — it can swallow exceptions silently.

items.q: What is try-with-resources in Java?
items.a: try-with-resources (Java 7+) automatically closes resources implementing AutoCloseable when the try block exits. Multiple resources are declared separated by semicolons and closed in reverse order. If both the try body and close() throw exceptions, the body's exception propagates and the close() exception is suppressed (accessible via getSuppressed()). This is the recommended pattern for all resource management, replacing verbose try-finally blocks.
